To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high ferritin levels and low glycosylation of ferritin are markers of excessive macrophages activation.
high ferritin level associated with low percentage of glycolated ferritin may be a marker for excessive macrophage activity in patients with hemophagocytic syndrome.
high ferritin level combined with low percentage of glyco-ferritin is a marker of excessive activation of the monocyte-macrophage system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the glycosylated and nonglycosylation ferritin in HS and in ASD.
the study of the ferritin level, the percentage of glycolysed ferritin, and the ferritin index in a series of patients with various causes of HS.
the use of ferritin as a marker of macrophage activation in the HS series.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high ferritin level associated with a low percentage (< 20%) of glycosylation is a marker of excessive and/or abnormal macrophage activation, which can be found in various conditions.
the combination of high ferritine levels and a low percentage of glycylated ferritine (<20%) is a marker of excessive phagocytic activity.
the percentage of glycolated ferritin is not a marker of the etiology of the HS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of high serum ferritin level and of low glycosylation percentage may be a marker for HS.
the combination of high ferritine levels and low percentage of glycated ferritine is a specific marker of HS.
ferritin is a marker of macrophage activation and that its glycosylation is a marker of its intracellular localization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the percentage of glycolysed ferritin is a marker of macrophage activation in the HS series.
the percentage of glyco ferritin may be a marker to differentiate between ASD and HS.
ferritin and glycosylation of ferritin should be considered as an early marker of excessive macrophase activation in patients with hemophagocytic syndrome.
